title: Identifying Neurodegeneration Along the Path of Intracranial CST in ALS Patients using Combined Metabolic and Microstructural Tractometry
text:
This project introduces a novel multiparametric image analytical method for diagnosis and evaluating disease
severity, upper motor neuron dysfunction, and neurocognitive impairment in patients with amyotrophic lateral
sclerosis (ALS). We will perform a voxel-wise fusion of whole-brain spectroscopic imaging and diffusion MRI
data along the intracranial corticospinal tract (CST) and generate multiple parametric tract profiles using a
tractometry framework. The simultaneous and spatially concordant assessment of metabolic and microstructural
abnormalities from distinct anatomical regions of intracranial CST will provide a more comprehensive
characterization of ALS disease for diagnostic and prognostic use.

title: Regulation of non-histone protein function by lysine methylation
text:
Lysine methylation is a widespread posttranslational modification, and the enzymes responsible for adding and
removing lysine methylation are dysregulated in many human diseases. While we understand much about lysine
methylation on histone proteins, thousands of non-histone proteins are also methylated. Our research aims to
determine how non-histone lysine methylation regulates protein function and ultimately impacts cellular
processes.

title: Genetic variation in genes controlling sperm-egg interactions in reproductively isolated populations of Astyanax mexicanus
text:
This research will uncover molecular factors essential for maintaining sperm-egg compatibility, biological
fitness, and successful fertilization by capitalizing on selective forces on gene function in a rapidly evolving and
readily cross-hybridizing fish model, Astyanax mexicanus. With a unique and tractable experimental platform,
we will be able to functionally characterize selected, hybridization sensitive sperm-egg interface genes. As
such molecular regulation paradigms are generally conserved in metazoans, these findings will enhance
understanding of egg and sperm biology and provide metrics of gamete quality and fertilization success
predictability.

title: Developing a Synthetic Adeno-Associated Virus (AAV) for Engineering Safer Gene Therapies
text:
Recombinant adeno-associated virus (rAAV) gene therapies are increasingly becoming a viable
treatment option for incurable genetic disorders. However, they are not without toxicity or significant risk, with
several rAAV-related deaths and numerous adverse outcomes reported during the past few years alone.
Embarking on a new research direction, we will utilize our complimentary expertise in neuroscience, stem cell
biology, and engineering to develop new methods for rAAV production and create the first rAAVs with engineered
inverted terminal repeats (ITRs) that are safer for human gene therapy.

title: OPTimizing surveillance in lung cancer survivors with novel IMAging biomarkers and deep-Learning (OPTIMAL)
text:
The proposed study will comprehensively evaluate patterns of imaging surveillance, characterize the benefits
and harms of imaging surveillance, develop and validate risk prediction models that incorporate imaging
biomarkers, and adapt a deep learning model to predict subsequent risk for lung cancer recurrence or SPLC
using CT images in lung cancer survivors. These results have the potential to inform patient and clinician
shared decision-making conversations to guide individualized surveillance strategies. As the number of lung
cancer survivors rises due to increased growth, aging, and the detection of early-stage lung cancer with
screening uptake, this research is timely and responsive to the National Cancer Institute’s goal to identify
optimal evidence-based schedules for surveillance of recurrence and progression and to generate better
estimates of risk and potential benefit for surveillance practices.

title: Biomarker based classification and clustering of Veterans with PTSD
text:
PTSD is a serious psychiatric concern for our Veteran population and the VA is highly
motivated to address our current gaps in understanding regarding the biological
underpinnings of stress response to traumatic experiences. Leveraging advancements in
genetics and brain functioning research may be an important path in improving this
understanding. This proposal looks to use publicly available datasets and empirically
derived biological markers for PTSD. We provide evidence this approach could help in
diagnosing PTSD, as well as uncovering different types of PTSD based on genetic and
brain data. This work could pave the way for algorithmically determining care, or
provide a foundation for developing tailored care for types of PTSD.

title: ADVANCING GENE-EDITING NUCLEASES FOR DIVERSE ZEBRAFISH APPLICATIONS
text:
Gene editing utilizes a collection of molecular technologies to change the genetic sequences in cells or
organisms. Although extremely useful, gene editing technologies have several limitations, including difficulties
controlling the number and location of insertions produced during transgenesis, and limitations in the scale and
throughput of genome editing in lab animals such as zebrafish. This proposal seeks to address these
limitations by developing several new gene editing technologies based on DNA integrases and CRISPR
nucleases.

title: An Ecological Momentary Assessment Study of Appearance-Related Safety Behaviors
text:
Appearance concerns represent a key factor present in multiple psychiatric disorders that contribute to a major
public health burden. Appearance related safety behaviors (ARSBs) represent a risk factor for the development
and maintenance of body dysmorphic disorder, eating disorders, and social anxiety disorder; however,
research has yet to identify how these behaviors fluctuate within a day, how these changes affect subsequent
symptoms, and what precedes the use of these behaviors. This study has the potential to provide a better
understanding of how these behaviors may be a response to certain situational triggers and how they affect
different symptoms in daily life.

title: Neuro-immune mechanisms in mutant IDH1 gliomas
text:
Mutant IDH1 gliomas harbor a better prognosis, and are more prevalent in younger patients. Nevertheless,
these tumors always recur, exhibiting higher mutational burden and displaying a more aggressive behavior.
The goals of this project are to uncover neuroimmunology-mediated mechanisms that could be harnessed for
therapeutic intent.

title: Proteomics-driven analysis and robotics-enabled drug testing of microdissected tumors and their microenvironment
text:
A major challenge in oncology has been to develop platforms that permit testing of therapies that are dependent
on the tumor microenvironment, such as combination therapies. We will use a robotic approach based on
microfluidic lifting-and-placing of cuboidal microdissected tumors (“cuboids”) that allows for testing combination
therapies in 384-well plates. The precision and reliability of our platform enables high-throughput treatment and
proteomics profiling of mouse and human cuboids.

title: Evolving together, evolving apart: probing the genomic basis of a facultative host-microbe mutualism
text:
Microbes significantly impact host health, for good and ill. While much research has focused on the evolution of
pathogens interacting with hosts, we lack comparable research on the considerable role that beneficial
microbes play in protecting and enhancing host health and stabilizing basic organismal functions. By
conducting fundamental research on host-microbe mutualisms in a system with an extensive genetic toolkit for
both organisms, this proposal will identify the genomic basis of adaptation of microbes inside and outside of
hosts and create a framework that will improve the ability to predict microbial host specialization and the
stability of host benefits.

title: Endothelial Cell SR-BI Regulation and Novel Protein Partners in Atherosclerosis
text:
Atherosclerosis underlies life-threatening cardiovascular disorders such as heart attack and stroke, and we
previously discovered that a specific protein in blood vessel lining cells binds LDL to carry it into the artery wall
to cause the atherosclerosis. We recently found that the amount of the protein in the lining cells is increased by
high cholesterol or turbulent blood flow, and that it has partner proteins required for the LDL transport. The
proposed research program will determine how the abundance of the protein is regulated by high cholesterol or
turbulent blood flow, and how the partner proteins work with it to participate in atherosclerosis development.

title: The distributed basis of visual cortical variability
text:
Processing visual information is a key nervous system function for many animals. However, understanding the
neural computations that underlie visual processing has been difficult due to large variability in these circuits.
The aim of this proposal is to leverage modern electrophysiological and computational approaches to map and
probe the distributed brain network underlying visual processing.

title: Core C - Proteomics Core
text: ABSTRACT – CORE C Core C will be responsible for the in-depth determination of the molecular composition, temporal dynamics and functional properties of the antibodies that comprise the polyclonal response to influenza HA or to SARS-CoV2 S in peripheral blood and in the respiratory track, following infection or vaccination. Core C will also perform the comprehensive sequencing and functional analyses of the natively paired VH:VL BCR repertoire encoded by B cell subsets of interest from peripheral blood, lymph node FNA, bone marrow aspirates and from respiratory track specimens. Both the IgG and the IgA serological and BCR repertoires will be determined and compared. Furthermore, we will analyze the immunoglobulin subclass repertoires. The studies by Core C will be enabled by a set of technologies developed by the UT Austin team, namely Ig-Seq: bottom-up high resolution LC-MS/MS based identification and quantification of antigen-specific circulating antibodies: BCR-Seq:very high throughput sequencing of natively paired VH and VL cDNA from single B cells and HuRep: extensive functional analysis of the B cell encoded repertoire displayed on yeast. Core C, together with Projects 1 and 2, will seek to address a plethora of key questions on the humoral responses to infection by respiratory pathogens and also following vaccination, including: (i) How does the sequence and functional diversity of the peripheral blood antibody repertoire compares to those of respiratory track antibodies? (ii) What fraction of the mucosal antibodies develop locally and are produced by tissue resident plasma cells versus being produced at other anatomical locations and then exported to the respiratory track following transcytosis from peripheral blood? (iii) What is the temporal persistence of individual IgG/IgA antibody clones in the respiratory track? (iv) To what extent does the concentration of individual IgG antibodies in peripheral blood correlates with their level in the mucosa following transcytosis via FcRn? Also, a related question is whether there exist abundant centrally produced antibodies that are not found in the respiratory track, either because of poor transepithelial export or enhanced mucosal elimination (e.g. due to proteolysis). (v) How do B cell clonal expansions in peripheral blood, lymph node aspirates and in the bone marrow correlate with the concentration of the respective antibody in circulation and in BALF? Finally, (iv) very importantly, together with Project 1 we will delineate the binding and neutralization breadth of the dominant anti-HA or anti-SARS-CoV2 antibodies in circulation and in the respiratory track.

title: Immunologic Mechanisms and Rheumatic Diseases
text:
The Division of Rheumatology, Inflammation, and Immunity at Brigham and Women’s Hospital and this training
grant vehicle provide the core that integrates basic and translational investigators across Harvard-affiliated
institutions working in areas of basic biology, and translational and population sciences. Themes are relevant to
and focused in musculoskeletal and autoimmune rheumatic disease. The goal is to provide an ongoing pipeline
of select, highly trained and expert investigators prepared for and focused on rheumatic disease research.

title: A Platform for Antifungal Discovery
text:
Fungal infections are on the rise due to the spread of drug resistance. The arsenal of
antifungals is small, and mortality due to disseminated fungal infections is 50%. In this project,
we will establish an efficient platform for discovery of novel antifungals, based on ultra-high-
throughput screening of soil bacterial producers in microdroplets, at a rate of 1 million an hour.

title: MR Fingerprinting for Epilepsy
text:
In this project, we aim to improve postoperative seizure outcomes for patients with pharmacoresistant focal
epilepsies and nonlesional MRI, by incorporating cutting-edge MR Fingerprinting (MRF) technology into clinical
practice. We will use MRF images to train machine/deep-learning models to identify epileptogenic brain
regions, thereby refining individualized surgical plans. Moreover, by merging MRF with SEEG data from our
patients, we will elucidate the complex interplay between quantitative MR imaging, pathology, and brain
physiological activity.

title: Restoring Vascular Integrity with PLGA-Encapsulated PTEN Nanoparticles: A Multi-Pathway Strategy to Prevent Restenosis and Atherosclerotic Progression
text:
Cardiovascular disease (CVD), particularly coronary artery disease, is a major chronic disease and a leading
cause of death, and current treatments fail to fully address the underlying issues like restenosis and thrombosis.
This research proposes using engineered nanoparticles to deliver PTEN, a key regulator of smooth muscle cell
function, to prevent harmful changes in blood vessel cells, reducing inflammation and cell overgrowth. By
targeting specific vascular cells with PTEN-encapsulated nanoparticles, this approach aims to improve long-term
outcomes in CVD treatment by reducing restenosis and supporting proper vascular repair.

title: Core B - Retrotransposon Genomics, Technology and Analysis Core
text: Core Summary Core B will provide cutting edge tools to measure retrotransposition in multicellular eukaryotes in the context of aging paradigms with a special focus on Alzheimer’s disease and related disorders. In addition to providing appropriate existing assays and mouse models to all of the participants, the core will also develop improved retrotransposition reporters and genomics tools to enable the detection and mapping of retrotransposition events in the various experimental systems under study. The Core will also provide “Driver systems” that lead to high level expression of these elements in both cell systems and animals. Finally, the core will provide cutting edge sequencing and computational tools to analyze both retrotransposition itself and the aberrant forms of LINE-1 expression and reverse transcription observed in aging cells and organisms.

title: Biostatistics, Bioinformatics, and Research Informatics Shared Resource
text: BIOSTATISTICS, BIOINFORMATICS, & RESEARCH INFORMATICS SR (BBRISR) The Biostatistics, Bioinformatics, & Research Informatics Shared Resource (BBRISR) plays a major role in collaborative efforts and project leadership across the Sidney Kimmel Cancer Center (SKCC) and provides SKCC investigators and other Shared Resources (SR) with centralized access to high-quality, state-of-the-art data collection, management, and analytic services through a coordinated, multi-faceted data science team. The SR was founded as the Biostatistics Shared Resource (BSR) in 1994 and has been continuously funded by the CCSG since 2001. In 2022, the BSR was expanded to incorporate capabilities in Bioinformatics (previously located in the MetaOmics SR) and Research Informatics (previously located in the Translational Pathology SR) to avoid duplication of efforts, enhance collaboration among computational staff, and provide a centralized resource for all data management and analytic needs. The BBRISR provides guidance on study design, database building and integration of diverse data types, development of statistical and bioinformatics analyses for grant applications and clinical/translational protocols, data analysis, and preparation of reports and manuscripts. The BBRISR supports investigators in all basic, translational, clinical, and population research activities and plays a critical role in SKCC community outreach and engagement, education, and training. The BBRISR is led by Co-Directors Benjamin Leiby, PhD and Christopher McNair, PhD. Leiby is Director of the Division of Biostatistics in the Department of Pharmacology, Physiology, and Cancer Biology. He previously served as Director of the BSR. McNair is Associate Director for Data Science for SKCC. As a large, newly expanded SR, complementary expertise of the Co-Directors allows optimal oversight of all components of BBRISR. The BBRISR is located in office suites in the Edison Building and 833 Chestnut, readily accessible to all SKCC members via a short walk (<1 mile). The Specific Aims of the BBRISR are to: 1) Support cancer research data analytics, 2) Manage cancer research informatics and data, and 3) Provide education and training to SKCC members, staff, and trainees. During the project period, the BBRISR served 129 SKCC members, 66 (51.2%) of which had peer-reviewed funding, representing all four Research Programs. BBRISR services were utilized by 154 total users in 199 peer reviewed publications (average impact factor 8.36), 250 grant applications (41 funded, 43 pending), and 82 clinical trials. In line with the SKCC strategic plan, IMPACT PHL, the BBRISR has set goals for targeted recruitment in four areas: 1) Faculty and staff in Bioinformatics, 2) Faculty with expertise in Informatics and analysis of Electronic Medical Record (EMR) data, 3) Biostatistics faculty with expertise in causal inference for observational data, and 4) Staff project manager to assist the Co-Directors with day-to-day operations and ensure timely delivery of services.
